Also, Chrome and Firefox both clamp the new playback position to within (0..duration) before exiting the currentTime setter, so presumably steps 6 and 7 (perhaps 8 as well?) should not be run in parallel, and be followed by setting of the current playback position (without side effects). Unless, of course, we want `videoA.currentTime = videoB.currentTime = Number.MAX_VALUE` to result in both videos always seeking to the end of their corresponding media resource.

However, step 9 for approximate-for-speed absolutely should be run in parallel, as the requirement to find a keyframe before or after the new playback position may in some situations take a not insignificant amount of time.

Another random thing worth noting, both Firefox and Safari "break" spec by seeking exactly to the new playback position when approximate-for-speed is set (in Firefox only when seeking forward), so the phrasing should probably allow for both seeking backward and forward to result in seeking to the exact position requested.

Ah, looks like I missed a small but important piece of information: setting `currentTime` is supposed to set the official playback position to the new playback position. So, to my reading, things are inconsistent in two regards:

- In existing browsers, the value of an expression setting `currentTime` is the value it was set to (expected, given the above), but the value returned by `currentTime` immediately after setting it is clamped to the playable range of the media. However, the spec's steps to seek don't contain any step to update the official playback position before resuming the script, so according to this, the new playback position within the media timeline should not be visible through the `currentTime` attribute returning the official playback position.
- In Firefox and Safari, calling `fastSeek()` results in `currentTime` returning the value passed to it, again moved within the valid media timeline.

Therefore, perhaps setting the `currentTime` value should be said to _return_ the value it was set to, rather than changing the official playback position. Then, the seeking steps could determine the new playback position according to the earliest playback position, the duration, and the seekable ranges, and then assign the official playback position to that.

There's a theoretical reason why the model in the spec makes sense. All playback information on media elements, notably including the seekable ranges, are a copy of information in the media pipeline, potentially on another thread or process. A seek request is therefore best handled by sending it to the media pipeline where the up-to-date information exists.

However, if all implementations actually clamp to `seekable` synchronously, then I think the spec should just align with this, and if it were ever a problem that potentially stale ranges are used, then it would need to be solved with a new method in the spec.

I had the same thought as well when I discovered this. After looking into the implementations further, it seems like they don't totally agree on what to do here either, unfortunately:

- Chromium runs all the steps synchronously up to the point where the target time is sent off to the player implementation. The step saying to run the subsequent steps in parallel is completely omitted: https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/media/html_media_element.cc;l=2682-2689;drc=4fc13c5ad1a034be2e6528404cc569b51c7b9299
    - It's worth noting that it doesn't implement fast seeking, but if it did, ignoring this step would definitely be a problem, since that would require the media pipeline to synchronously provide a keyframe position.
- Firefox clamps to the `seekable` only, and doesn't explicitly name any steps: https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/rev/b333202cd8d8385cb382c42404a03995dbc126ec/dom/media/mediaelement/HTMLMediaElement.cpp#3678-3720
    - They also mention that the spec requires the new position to be reflected but make an exception for the approximate for speed step, which makes me think that doing this synchronously was an accident, unless the step to make this asynchronous was added after their implementation.
- WebKit only clamps to the duration: https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/73aa6c8/Source/WebCore/html/HTMLMediaElement.cpp#L4051

I think my pull request already implements this closest to Chromium while leaving room for `fastSeek()` to asynchronously determine the requisite target.

Would that phrasing not be referring to the new value of `currentTime` rather than the new position calculated by the seeking steps? That would imply that it would not synchronously reflect the clamping. Not only that, but it also means that `fastSeek()` doesn't set the official playback position, so `video.fastSeek(n); console.log(video.currentTime)` would print the previous time rather than the seek steps' new playback position, which is not what Firefox does.

It's also worth noting that even if setting the current playback position was done synchronously, the official playback position would still not update to reflect that, since it has to await a stable state first. If an implementer interprets those steps as synchronous, the clamped position should still not be reflected unless the `currentTime` setter is inserting itself into the seeking steps.

It does. The clamping to the nearest seekable is in the asynchronous steps. When this actually happens is non-predictable. 

I do believe that this bug should be closed. There's nothing to fix in the spec.

> It does. The clamping to the nearest seekable is in the asynchronous steps. When this actually happens is non-predictable.

The spec says that the official playback position should only reflect the current playback position when we reach a stable state. That implies that it shouldn't be visible to JS immediately after a seek is initiated. As I said, that's not what browsers do, and also means that `fastSeek()` should not be visible immediately unless it is at least changed to match the `currentTime` setter. If we want to keep the spec as it is, I would argue that all implementations need to change to stop reporting the clamped value synchronously, and only apply that change after the current task ends to reach a stable state.

However, I don't think it makes sense to leave it to implementers to decide what `currentTime` reflects immediately after a seek. That just allows `currentTime` to change out-of-turn, which makes its behavior very unpredictable around seeks.

> Clamping to the seekable range is per spec and in the seeking algorithm.

To be clear, I was never saying that clamping to the seekable range is where they differ, just in whether it becomes exposed in the same JS task.

I feel like I haven't explained my case too clearly since I didn't get enough sleep, but this is what I understand the spec to be asking for:

```js
console.log(video.duration); // 5
console.log(video.currentTime); // 0
video.currentTime = 10;
console.log(video.currentTime); // spec: 10; chromium/firefox/webkit: 5
setTimeout(0, () {
  console.log(video.currentTime); // spec: 10 or 5 depending on parallel steps' execution; chromium/firefox/webkit: 5
});
video.addEventListener("seeked", () {
  console.log(video.currentTime); // 5
});
```

Tracing the spec steps at a high level:
1. We start with current playback position and official playback position set to 0, media duration is 5.
2. The first log of `currentTime` reads the official playback position of 0.
3. `video.currentTime = 10` sets the official playback position to 10
4. Seeking steps begin, let's assume they synchronously set the _current_ playback position to 5 before waiting for the new position to be established.
5. The second log of `currentTime` reads the _official_ playback position, which notably has not mirrored the current playback position yet, as we haven't reached microtask checkpoint, so it produces 10.
6. `setTimeout()` is called, causing a task to run at the next event loop iteration.
7. The event loop reaches a microtask checkpoint, so the official playback position now mirrors the current playback position of 5.
8. The timeout is reached, and the log of `currentTime` reads the new official playback position of 5.
9. The log in the `seeked` event also produces 5.

In a case where we invoke `fastSeek(10)` instead of assigning `currentTime`:

```js
console.log(video.duration); // 5
console.log(video.currentTime); // 0
video.fastSeek(10);
console.log(video.currentTime); // spec: 0; firefox/webkit: 5
setTimeout(0, () {
  console.log(video.currentTime); // spec: 0 or 5 depending on parallel steps' execution; firefox/webkit: always 5
});
video.addEventListener("seeked", () {
  console.log(video.currentTime); // 5
});
```

1. We start with current playback position and official playback position set to 0, media duration is 5.
2. The first log of `currentTime` reads the official playback position of 0.
3. `video.fastSeek(10)` is called, does nothing outside invoking the seeking steps with the approximate-for-speed flag set.
4. Seeking steps begin, let's assume they synchronously set the current playback position to 5 before waiting for the new position to be established.
5. The second log of `currentTime` reads the official playback position, which hasn't mirrored the current playback position, so it produces the initial 0.
6. `setTimeout()` is called, causing a task to run at the next event loop iteration.
7. The event loop reaches a microtask checkpoint, so the official playback position now mirrors the current playback position of 5.
8. The timeout callback is invoked and reads `currentTime`, producing the official playback position of 5.
9. The log in the `seeked` event also produces 5.

As I've noted in the JS snippets, implementations make `currentTime` reflect the synchronously-chosen current playback position in the same task. In WebKit at least, this isn't because it assigns to any equivalent of the official playback position, but rather because while a seek is ongoing, the `currentTime` getter explicitly returns the chosen seek target.

What I'm suggesting here is that we make this explicit in some form or another:
- Set the official playback position to the new playback position in the seeking steps so that `fastSeek()` actually affects `currentTime`. This leaves room for `currentTime` to shift while the seek is ongoing if the clamps are not done synchronously.
- Use a separate variable (seeking playback position?) to track what the seek chose, and prefer that over the official playback position in the `currentTime` getter. This makes `currentTime` completely stable while `seeking === true`, which seems like a nice property to me.

The media WPT (those were mostly from chrome's own test" do test the wrong thing on closer look:
wpt/html/semantics/embedded-content/media-elements/seeking/seek-to-max-value.htm sets v.currentTime = Number.MAX_VALUE and immediately asserts v.currentTime == v.seekable.end(0). That requires synchronous clamping, which contradicts the literal spec, where the value would read back as MAX_VALUE.

Step 11 only affects the "current playback position" not the "official playback position"; so you should only read back the original position at the next stable state at step 13 and so only be updated when the seeking attribute is set to false (not when the seeked event handlers would actually run which is at the next event loop)

Now that isn't what the existing user agents implement, but the spec itself is on its own is correct and not racy. There's no room for interpretation which to me is what specs are about

webkit in particular will return m_lastSeekTime if set, so reading the currentTime while the seeking is ongoing will show changing values; including when clamping occurred: that's not per spec.

user agent implementation bugs don't always correlate with spec bugs, you seem to mix the two in the various issues you've opened. 
WPT should be written to test the spec, not to comply with what a particular implementation is doing.

Now in this particular case, it may be opened to discussion to determine if the spec as written make sense in the real world. 

We could discuss this next month at the 2026 TPAC.

Indeed, I agree that it's not totally clear the right solution here. My assumption was that given three implementations all produce the clamped value in the same task, it would be safer to match that than to attempt to change their behaviors.

I think that at the very least, `fastSeek()` needs some consideration here, though, it's odd for it to behave differently to `currentTime`.

I should also note that at the same time that `currentTime` synchronously reflects the clamp above, implementations will also have cleared `ended`, which also disagrees with the spec, where it should only change at event loop step 1. I have a suspicion that some MSE players may depend on this behavior, but I'll have to try to find confirmation.

Thanks for having a look!
